% ====================================================================
% ABSTRACT — M5 writes
% ====================================================================
\begin{abstract}
Hydrate formation in offshore well service lines can cause costly shutdowns
and safety hazards if not detected early. This study compares three models
--- XGBoost (feature-engineered baseline), a Temporal Convolutional Network
(TCN), and a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) --- for early warning of hydrate
events using Petrobras's 3W Dataset~2.0.0 (Event~9). All three models are
evaluated at a matched false-alarm budget of one alarm per 100 operating
hours, with lead time (time from first alarm to annotated transient onset)
as the headline metric. Each model is trained under two conditions:
real-only and real-plus-simulated data. We employ grouped cross-validation
with well-level splits to prevent data leakage. Our results demonstrate that
XGBoost trained exclusively on real data achieved the highest event recall of $23.3\%$ ($\pm 25.2\%$) and a mean lead time of $43.4$\,min across the two folds where any event was detected, at a matched false-alarm rate of $1.0\%$/h.
Deep models (TCN and GRU) did not reliably detect events on the held-out test wells in any condition, primarily because only 14 real transient instances are available for training and evaluation.
Simulated data did not improve performance for any model.
The feature-engineered baseline remains the only approach that demonstrates non-trivial detection on this dataset.

Reproduction: all code, data processing, and evaluation are available at
\url{https://github.com/AMammedova/team-hydrate3w}.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
hydrate formation, early warning, time series classification,
temporal convolutional network, gated recurrent unit, 3W dataset
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

% TODO (M1): Write the Introduction section. Should cover:
% - Motivation: hydrate formation in offshore wells, safety & economic impact
% - The 3W Dataset as a benchmark for early warning in O&G
% - Brief summary of Event 9 (hydrate in service line)
% - Research question: can DL models provide earlier warning than classical baselines?
% - Paper structure overview (one sentence per section)

Hydrate formation in subsea well service lines is a critical operational hazard in offshore oil and gas production. When gas hydrates crystallize inside flowlines they can cause complete blockages, requiring costly well shutdowns, intervention operations, and posing safety risks to personnel and equipment~\cite{sleiman}. Early detection of the transient phase — the initial stage before full blockage — gives operators actionable lead time to apply thermodynamic or chemical inhibition before the line is lost.

The Petrobras 3W Dataset~2.0.0~\cite{3w} provides a rare public benchmark for this problem. Event~9 (hydrate formation in service lines) contains 57 real well instances, 150 simulated instances, and 594 normal-operation instances. However, a careful inspection of the real instances reveals that \textbf{only 14 of the 57 real instances contain a transient phase}; only 3 reach full blockage. This makes Event~9 one of the most statistically challenging classification problems in the 3W collection: the positive class is not just rare, it is nearly absent in the test wells of any cross-validation fold.

This paper asks whether modern deep sequence models — a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN)~\cite{tcn} and a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU)~\cite{gru} — can detect hydrate onset earlier than a feature-engineered XGBoost baseline~\cite{xgboost}, given the severe data scarcity. We evaluate all three models under two training conditions (real-only vs.~real-plus-simulated) at a matched false-alarm budget of one alarm per 100 operating hours, using grouped cross-validation with well-level splits to prevent data leakage.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:dataset} describes the 3W dataset and the measured properties of Event~9. Section~\ref{sec:related_work} reviews related work. Section~\ref{sec:method} defines the models and feature extraction. Section~\ref{sec:experimental_setup} describes the cross-validation design and simulation policy. Section~\ref{sec:results} reports experimental results. Section~\ref{sec:discussion} discusses limitations, and Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes.

\section{Dataset}
\label{sec:dataset}

% TODO (M1): Write the Dataset section. Must include all numbers from

\subsection{Dataset Overview}
The 3W Dataset 2.0.0~\cite{3w} is a publicly available benchmark for undesirable event detection in oil wells. For Event~9 (hydrate formation in service lines), the dataset provides 57 real instances, 150 simulated instances, and 594 normal-operation instances, each a multivariate time series recorded at 1\,Hz from up to 8 process sensors (pressures and temperatures along the wellbore and service line).

\subsection{Event-9 Properties}
\textbf{Severity monotonicity.} All 57 real instances are monotonically increasing in severity: once a well enters the Transient phase it never returns to Normal, and once it enters the Established (blocked) phase it never returns to Transient. This was verified programmatically. The property validates our label encoding as ordinal and justifies measuring lead time to the first irreversible state change.

\textbf{Scarcity of the positive class.} Only 14 of the 57 real instances contain a Transient phase; only 3 reach the Established (blockage) state. The transient phase is therefore our headline target: measuring lead time to blockage onset would cover only 3 events, an insufficient sample for any statistical claim. The 14 transient-phase instances span 7 distinct wells.

\textbf{Missingness and dead sensors.} NaN labels appear in all 57 real instances (median 11.2\%, maximum 50.4\% of samples in a channel). Three instances carry sensors that are completely dead for the entire recording (P-TPT and T-TPT frozen at constant values). These are detected by a frozen-sensor scan and the corresponding mask entries are set to 0 before windowing.

\textbf{Channel selection.} We evaluated two channel subsets: a 5-channel arm (\texttt{P-PDG, P-TPT, T-TPT, P-MON-CKP, T-JUS-CKP}) and a 7-channel arm that additionally includes annular sensors. All 14 transient events and all 3 blockage events survive both selections. The 5-channel arm was retained because the additional annular channels are absent in roughly 30\% of real instances, which would inflate the missingness fraction without contributing coverage.

\subsection{Preprocessing}
\textbf{Decimation and windowing.} Raw 1\,Hz signals are decimated to one sample per 30\,s, reducing noise without losing event-scale information. Windows of $W=60$ decimated samples (30 minutes) are extracted with a stride of 5 samples (150\,s). The \textbf{median real instance} contains 32{,}135 timesteps at 1\,Hz; at the decimated rate this yields roughly 1{,}071 windows per instance, well above the minimum needed to train a causal model.

\textbf{Labeling.} Each window is assigned the most severe label present in any of its 60 samples (\texttt{most\_severe} rule). This is the correct choice: a window that ends in Established phase but whose first samples were still Transient must be reported as Established, because the last state is the one that matters operationally.

\textbf{Per-instance normalization.} Each channel is normalized using the mean and standard deviation of its \emph{own} instance, computed over present samples only. This is mandatory, not cosmetic: the 15 hydrate wells and the 9 normal-operation wells are disjoint populations with no well in common. A model that sees raw absolute pressures could simply memorize which pressure range belongs to which population — per-instance normalization removes that shortcut from the value space. Sensor absence (the mask) remains and is treated separately.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{annotated_trace.png}
\caption{Annotated multivariate sensor trace of a real Event-9 instance. Colour bands indicate operational regimes: Normal, Transient, and Established blockage. Early warning evaluates alarm lead time before the transient onset.}
\label{fig:annotated_trace}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Cache statistics.} The built cache contains \textbf{42{,}259 real windows} from 364 usable real instances, of which 1{,}295 are Transient and 118 Established, giving a positive rate of 3.34\%. The simulated arm adds 43{,}829 windows, of which 90.3\% are positive — a distribution radically different from the real data.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related_work}

% TODO (M4): Write Related Work. Should cover:
% - TCN for industrial time-series classification (Bai et al., 2018)
% - GRU for sequence modeling (Cho et al., 2014)
% - Early warning systems in process industries
% - 3W dataset prior work (Vargas et al.)

\subsection{Sequence Models for Industrial Fault Detection}
Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCN)~\cite{tcn} have demonstrated strong performance on a wide range of sequence classification benchmarks, matching or outperforming LSTM and GRU-based models while offering easier parallelization during training. The key design choice is the use of causal dilated convolutions, which expand the receptive field exponentially with depth without introducing future information into any prediction. This causal property is not merely a convenience: in a real early-warning system, any operation that looks beyond the current time step would inflate the reported lead time, making the system appear more capable than it is in deployment.

Gated Recurrent Units (GRU)~\cite{gru} provide a simpler alternative to LSTM with fewer parameters. Like TCN, the GRU processes sequences step-by-step and is causal by construction when used in a unidirectional configuration. We use unidirectional GRU exclusively; a bidirectional GRU would introduce future context and invalidate the lead-time metric.

\subsection{Prior Work on the 3W Dataset}
Vargas et al.~\cite{3w} introduced the 3W dataset and demonstrated that classical machine learning methods (Random Forests, k-NN) achieve competitive performance on Event~9, but evaluated at the window level rather than the event level. Our evaluation protocol differs materially: we count \emph{event recall} (did any alarm fire before the annotated transient onset?) and measure \emph{lead time} (how early?), both of which are operationally meaningful quantities that window-level accuracy masks entirely. At a 3.34\% positive rate, a classifier that labels every window as Normal achieves 96.66\% window accuracy while missing every event.

\subsection{Early Warning in Process Control}
Process-industry early warning systems are reviewed in Qin~\cite{qin}, who notes that the dominant practical challenge is not algorithm design but the scarcity of labeled fault data: real process upsets are rare, expensive to induce, and often unrepeatable. This observation directly motivates our comparison of real-only vs.~real-plus-simulated training conditions and our conservative evaluation protocol.

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

% ---- IV-A. Feature Engineering (M3) ----
\subsection{Baseline Feature Engineering}
\label{sec:method_features}


The baseline is treated as a real competitor rather than a formality: it
receives the same folds, the same class-imbalance treatment and the same
calibration step as the deep models, and a recorded tuning budget. A
baseline that was never tuned would make the deep-model comparison
uninterpretable.

\subsubsection{Input}
The baseline consumes the same cache as the deep models: channels-first
\texttt{float32} $[N, C, W]$ windows with an aligned \texttt{uint8} presence
mask, where $\mathrm{mask}=1$ marks a genuinely observed sample. With the
main-arm channel set, $C=5$ and $W=60$ decimated samples at one sample per
30\,s, so each window spans \textbf{30 minutes} with a stride of 150\,s. On
the built cache this gives \textbf{42{,}259 real windows} from 364 usable
real instances, of which 1{,}295 are Transient and 118 Established --- a
positive rate of \textbf{3.34\%}. All 14 transient events and all 3 blockage
events survive the channel choice.

\subsubsection{Multi-timescale, mask-aware features}
For each window and channel we take three nested slices measured
\emph{from the end} of the window (the full 60 samples, the last 30, and the
last 15) and compute six statistics on each: mean, standard deviation,
minimum, maximum, least-squares slope, and the net change between the first
and last present sample. Taking slices from the end is what keeps the
features causal: a spike early in the window can only affect the full-window
statistics, which is verified by a unit test rather than assumed. Every
statistic is computed over \textbf{present samples only}, and the
per-channel presence fraction over the full window is appended as its own
feature block, so the model is told how much of each channel it is trusting.
With $C=5$ this yields $5 \times 6 \times 3 + 5 = 95$ features.

The extractor has no fitted state: every column is a function of one window
and its own mask, with no statistic pooled across rows. Extracting once for
the whole cache is therefore bit-identical to extracting per fold, and the
runner asserts the absence of a \texttt{fit()} at start-up so the property
cannot silently lapse.

\subsubsection{Encoding a dead sensor}
Three real instances carry sensors frozen for their entire recording, and one
of them is a blockage event, so this is not a corner case. When a channel
observes nothing, its statistics are undefined. Emitting $0.0$ is actively
wrong here: per-instance normalisation centres each recording near zero, so
$0.0$ is precisely the value a \emph{healthy} sensor at its own baseline
reports, and that encoding would state that a dead sensor looks normal. We
emit \texttt{NaN} and let XGBoost learn a default branch direction at each
split. The presence fraction remains a real measurement of exactly $0.0$ and
is never \texttt{NaN}. Similarly, the slope is regressed on each sample's
true position inside the slice rather than on its rank among present
samples, so a gap keeps its width and the slope remains a rate; regressing
on rank reports $9.0$ for two points nine steps apart rising nine units.
Section~\ref{sec:results_xgb} reports that neither change is separable from
fold noise on this cache, and we retain both on correctness grounds while
saying so explicitly.

\subsubsection{Class imbalance}
Imbalance is handled with inverse-frequency \texttt{sample\_weight} computed
from each training fold's own class counts. It is deliberately \emph{not}
handled with \texttt{scale\_pos\_weight}, which is a binary-classification
parameter in XGBoost and has no defined effect under
\texttt{multi:softprob} with \texttt{num\_class=3}. \texttt{num\_class=3} is
set explicitly rather than inferred, because a training fold can legitimately
contain no Established windows --- only 118 exist in the entire real cache
--- and the positive-score reduction indexes the third column.

\subsubsection{Tuning and calibration}
Hyperparameters are searched on the \textbf{training fold only}, scored by
grouped inner cross-validation over that fold's wells, across a 16-point
grid. Both conditions of a fold share the configuration selected on that
fold's real training wells, so \texttt{real\_only} and
\texttt{real\_plus\_sim} differ only in training data and not also in
hyperparameters. The scored quantity is validation PR-AUC on
$P(\mathrm{Transient}) + P(\mathrm{Established})$ --- the same reduction the
alarm logic consumes --- and sample weights are applied inside the search
exactly as at final fit time.

Because Module~8 selects the alarm threshold by sweeping a probability axis,
the probabilities must mean what they say. Weighted training on a 3\%
positive rate pushes scores away from the base rate by construction, so
miscalibration is expected rather than incidental. A Platt calibrator is fit
on the \textbf{validation} fold and applied \textbf{unchanged} to that fold's
test wells; Platt is preferred over isotonic because a validation fold holds
only a handful of positive events, where a non-parametric fit would track
noise.

% ---- IV-B. Architectures (M4) ----
\subsection{Model Architectures}
\label{sec:method_arch}

% TODO (M4): Describe TCN and GRU architectures.
% TCN: 4 temporal blocks, kernel_size=3, dilations [1,2,4,8],
%   receptive field = 61, channels-first input, mask concatenated
% GRU: unidirectional (causality), hidden_size=64, num_layers=1
%   mask concatenated on channel axis
% Both take (x, mask) explicitly per Addendum A.3

\subsubsection{Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN)}
The TCN consists of four temporal blocks with kernel size $k=3$ and dilation factors $d \in \{1, 2, 4, 8\}$. The receptive field of this architecture is:
\begin{equation}
    r = 1 + 2(k-1)\sum_{i} d_i = 1 + 2 \times 2 \times 15 = 61 \text{ samples}
\end{equation}
With $W=60$ samples per window, the receptive field of 61 exceeds the window length by one step, verified at runtime by the assertion \texttt{assert tcn.receptive\_field() >= window\_size}. Each temporal block applies a causal convolution followed by weight normalization and ReLU activation. The missingness mask is concatenated along the channel axis at the input layer, providing the model with explicit information about which sensor readings are reliable. The model outputs a 3-class softmax distribution and is trained with cross-entropy loss weighted by the inverse class frequency of the current training fold.

\subsubsection{Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU)}
The GRU classifier uses a single-layer unidirectional GRU with hidden size 64, followed by a linear readout layer producing a 3-class logit vector. The unidirectional constraint is non-negotiable: a bidirectional GRU would incorporate information from future time steps into the current prediction, inflating reported lead times and making the model inapplicable in real-time deployment. As with the TCN, the missingness mask is concatenated to the input at each timestep. Training uses the same class-weighted cross-entropy and early stopping on validation PR-AUC with patience of 10 epochs, saving the best checkpoint by validation PR-AUC.

% ---- IV-C. Evaluation Protocol (M5) ----
\subsection{Evaluation Protocol}
\label{sec:method_eval}

We evaluate all models using three complementary metrics at a matched
operating point:

\textbf{Lead Time.} For each hydrate event instance, lead time is defined as
the difference between the annotated transient onset time and the first alarm
onset that occurs before it:
\begin{equation}
    \text{lead\_time} = t_{\text{transient\_onset}} - t_{\text{first\_alarm}}
\end{equation}
Following the data analysis in Section~\ref{sec:dataset}, we use the
\emph{transient} onset (label code 109 in the 3W convention) rather than the
blockage onset, because only 3 of 57 real instances reach blockage. The
transient onset is available for all 14 positive-event instances across 7
wells.

\textbf{Event Recall.} The fraction of real hydrate events for which at least
one alarm onset occurs before the transient onset. A missed event (no alarm
before failure) contributes 0; a detected event contributes 1 regardless of
how many alarms fired.

\textbf{False Alarm Rate (FAR).} The number of alarm \emph{onsets} on
Normal-operation instances, divided by the total Normal operating hours in that
fold's test set:
\begin{equation}
    \text{FAR} = \frac{N_{\text{false\_alarm\_onsets}}}{\text{total\_normal\_hours}}
\end{equation}
Critically, we count alarm onsets, not individual windows above threshold —
one sustained false alarm counts as one event, not thousands
(Section~\ref{sec:method_eval}, pitfall W4.1).

\textbf{Operating Point.} All models are compared at a matched target FAR of
$1/100$ per operating hour. The threshold achieving this FAR is selected on
the \emph{validation} fold only (per-fold, per-model), then applied unchanged
to the test fold. This ``freeze'' protocol (S3 in our timeline) ensures that
test-set numbers are never used to tune any hyperparameter.

\textbf{Alarm Definition.} A positive-class probability $p(t)$ is first
smoothed with a causal (trailing) rolling mean of configurable window size.
An alarm fires when the smoothed probability stays above the selected
threshold for at least \texttt{min\_duration} continuous seconds. The causal
smoothing constraint is critical: a centered moving average would leak future
information into the current alarm decision, inflating lead time measurements
(see \texttt{tests/test\_alarm.py} for the regression test guarding this).

\textbf{Supplementary Metrics.} PR-AUC (area under the precision--recall
curve for the collapsed binary positive score), per-class PR-AUC
(Normal/Transient/Established one-vs-rest), and Expected Calibration Error
(ECE) are reported for completeness.

\subsection{Grouped Cross-Validation Design}
The fundamental challenge in designing cross-validation for this dataset is that the 15 hydrate wells and the 9 normal-operation wells are completely disjoint: no well appears in both sets. A standard \texttt{StratifiedGroupKFold} applied to the full dataset would create folds where the test set contains wells from one population and the training set contains wells from the other, making it impossible to properly balance both populations across folds simultaneously.

We therefore use \textbf{two independent grouped splits}: one over the 7 positive-event wells (by well ID) and one over the 9 normal-operation wells, balanced by available normal-operation hours rather than instance count (a single well contributes 1{,}220\,h, while another contributes only 6\,h). The two splits are then paired to form complete folds, each containing positive and normal test wells. Simulated instances are restricted to training folds in all experiments; they never appear in validation or test splits.

With only 7 positive wells, the maximum number of folds that guarantees at least 2 positive test wells per fold is \textbf{3 folds}. Table~\ref{tab:fold_report} reports the composition of each fold.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Fold composition. Each row is one test fold. \emph{Val. pos.\ events} is the number of positive-event instances in the validation split; this determines whether threshold selection is reliable. \emph{Test normal hours} is the denominator of the FAR calculation.}
\label{tab:fold_report}
\begin{tabular}{ccccc}
\toprule
Fold & Val.\ pos.\ events & Test pos.\ events & Test norm.\ hrs \\
\midrule
0 & 1 & 5 & 509.2 \\
1 & 3 & 5 & 556.8 \\
2 & 5 & 4 & 530.7 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Fold~0 has only one positive validation event, which makes the threshold sweep for that fold highly unreliable: with a single event, any threshold that happens to detect it is selected regardless of its behavior on Normal instances. This structural constraint is a property of the dataset with 7 positive wells, not a methodological error, and it contributes substantially to the high cross-fold variance reported in Section~\ref{sec:results_xgb}.

\subsection{Simulation Policy}
Simulated instances were added to the training set only for the \texttt{real\_plus\_sim} condition. The simulated set contains 150 instances with 43{,}829 windows, of which 90.3\% are positive — compared to 3.34\% in the real training data. This severe distributional mismatch is a confound that we track explicitly: the \texttt{real\_plus\_sim} condition inflates the training positive rate by a factor of $\approx$27, which changes the model's learned prior and can hurt its performance on the real test distribution. All threshold selection and calibration are performed on the real validation fold regardless of training condition.

\subsection{Compute Environment}
All experiments were run on the AI Academy shared A100 GPU (80\,GB VRAM). XGBoost training used CPU; deep model training used CUDA with automatic mixed precision (\texttt{torch.cuda.amp}). Reproducibility is ensured by seeding NumPy, PyTorch, and CUDA with \texttt{base\_seed + fold\_index} before each fold.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

% ---- VI-A. XGBoost Baseline Results (M3) ----
\subsection{XGBoost Baseline}
\label{sec:results_xgb}


\subsubsection{Validation performance}
Table~\ref{tab:xgb_folds} gives validation PR-AUC over the three grouped
folds at a positive-window base rate of $0.0334$.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{XGBoost validation PR-AUC per fold (seed 42). The standard
deviation exceeds the mean; see Section~\ref{sec:results_xgb} for why.}
\label{tab:xgb_folds}
\begin{tabular}{cccc}
\toprule
Fold & Positive val.\ events & \texttt{real\_only} & \texttt{real\_plus\_sim} \\
\midrule
0 & 1 & 0.0005 & 0.0003 \\
1 & 3 & \textbf{0.7755} & 0.2420 \\
2 & 5 & 0.0751 & 0.1288 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{2}{c}{mean $\pm$ sd} & $0.284 \pm 0.428$ & $0.124 \pm 0.121$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Simulated data did not help. The paired difference
(\texttt{real\_plus\_sim} $-$ \texttt{real\_only}) is $-0.160 \pm 0.325$,
negative in two of three folds. This is a distribution argument rather than
a sample-size one: the simulated windows are \textbf{90.3\%} positive
(39{,}561 of 43{,}829) against a \textbf{3.34\%} real positive rate, and they
inflate the training set from roughly 19k to 63k rows, pulling the model
toward a regime that does not exist in the real wells it is scored on.
\texttt{real\_only} is therefore the headline condition.

\subsubsection{PR-AUC is not comparable across these folds}
\label{sec:results_baserate}
Each fold's validation split has a different positive base rate, and PR-AUC
rises mechanically with it. Fold~0's validation set contains \textbf{exactly
one positive window} out of 11{,}260 (base rate $10^{-4}$), fold~1 has 463
of 7{,}327 ($0.0632$) and fold~2 has 638 of 11{,}592 ($0.0550$) --- more
than two orders of magnitude apart. A PR-AUC computed from a single positive
row is that row's reciprocal rank, not a performance estimate. Read as lift
over each fold's own base rate, the baseline is above chance in all three
folds ($1.4\times$, $12.3\times$, $3.5\times$) rather than at chance in two
of them, which is what the raw column suggests.

This is not a pedantic point, and we report it because the uncorrected
analysis is the natural one to run and it misleads. On raw PR-AUC the number
of positive validation events correlates strongly with score across the
ablation's 18 cells (Spearman $\rho = 0.638$, $p = 0.0044$), which invites
the conclusion that sparse folds cannot measure anything. That correlation
\textbf{does not survive base-rate correction}: on lift, $\rho = -0.14$
($p = 0.58$). Folds with more positive events also have higher base rates.
The same trap applies to any per-fold PR-AUC comparison in this project,
including the head-to-head model table.

\subsubsection{Fold composition dominates every other source of variance}
The feature ablation ran 9 extractor variants over 18 paired cells (3 CV
split seeds $\times$ 3 folds $\times$ 2 model seeds) on validation folds
only. Decomposing the variance across those 162 runs on the
base-rate-corrected scale, the variance of the feature-design arm means is
$2.09\times10^{-2}$ while the variance of the fold-cell means is $0.988$:
fold composition accounts for roughly \textbf{47$\times$} more spread than
the entire feature-design space we searched. (On the raw scale the ratio is
$448\times$, but part of that is the base-rate artifact above rather than
genuine instability.) Anything selected on validation PR-AUC in a
single-positive-window fold --- including the deep models' early stopping
and Module~8's threshold selection --- is selected on noise.

One training fold could not be tuned at all: in fold~1 every positive window
in the training split belongs to a \emph{single} well, so grouped inner
cross-validation cannot produce a split with positives on both sides. All
three inner splits were unusable and that fold fell back to the default
configuration. With 7 positive wells and 3 outer folds this is a structural
property of the dataset, not an accident of one seed.

\subsubsection{Feature-design ablation: null results}
Arms were compared as paired differences on identical folds and seeds and
tested with a Wilcoxon signed-rank test, restricted to the 10 cells where
validation PR-AUC is estimable, and expressed as base-rate-corrected lift
ratios per Section~\ref{sec:results_baserate}. The presence-fraction block
is worth $1.175\times$ (7/10 wins, $p = 0.027$); one timescale versus three
$1.027\times$ ($p = 0.92$); \texttt{NaN} versus $0.0$ encoding of a dead
sensor $1.025\times$ ($p = 0.77$); the slope's time axis $0.977\times$
($p = 0.63$); two timescales versus three $0.914\times$ ($p = 0.23$).

Only the presence-fraction block separates from noise, and it does so on
both the raw and corrected scales; everything else is within 3\% of parity.
Even that result would not survive a Bonferroni correction for the six
comparisons made ($p < 0.0083$), so we read it as suggestive --- but it is the only arm
where direction, win count and $p$-value agree, and
Section~\ref{sec:results_shortcut} supplies an independent mechanism for
why. We retain the two changed defaults on correctness grounds --- $0.0$ is
the value a healthy sensor at its own baseline reports, and a slope
regressed on sample rank is not a rate --- rather than claiming the numbers
supported them. Three timescales are kept because the module contract
specifies them; one timescale (35 features instead of 95) performs the same
within noise.

\subsubsection{The baseline partly reads instrumentation, not physics}
\label{sec:results_shortcut}
Gain importance on fold~1, the only fold with substantial validation signal,
placed \textbf{40.8\% of the total gain on the 5 presence-fraction columns}
out of 95. We tested the implication directly by training on those columns
\emph{only}, with no sensor values of any kind, over 9 fold-cells. The
presence-only model reaches a mean validation PR-AUC of \textbf{0.172}
against \textbf{0.233} for the full 95-feature model --- \textbf{74\% of the
full performance without seeing a single pressure or temperature reading}
--- and in 4 of 9 cells it \emph{outperforms} all 90 value features (0.493
versus 0.354; 0.284 versus 0.259; 0.093 versus 0.021; and 0.0008 versus
0.0006).

The explanation is in the dataset. Missingness here is well-specific:
different wells instrument different sensors, and some sensors are dead for
an entire instance. Because the hydrate wells and the Normal-operation wells
are disjoint populations, sensor availability is a proxy for well identity,
and well identity is very nearly the label. Per-instance normalisation, the
project's main defence against well-identity confounding, removes each
recording's offset and scale but cannot remove \emph{``this channel is
absent''}, which lives in the mask rather than in the values.

Consistently with this, permutation importance neither reproduces the
expected physical signature nor reproduces itself across folds: pairwise
rank agreement is nil (Kendall $\tau = +0.20, +0.40, -0.40$; all
$p > 0.48$). In fold~1 the top-ranked channel is \texttt{P-ANULAR}, the
annulus, which does not communicate with the service line, while
\texttt{P-MON-CKP} --- the pressure upstream of the production choke, which
the restriction mechanism predicts should dominate --- ranks last with a
mean share of $0.002$. \textbf{We therefore do not claim that the baseline
recovered the physical hydrate signature.} Claiming otherwise would have
required quoting one fold and ignoring the other two.

\subsubsection{The operating point, not the ranking, is what costs event recall}
\label{sec:results_frontier}
At the pre-registered budget of one false alarm per 100 operating hours the
baseline flags few events, and it is worth separating two possible causes:
a threshold chosen on validation that fails to transfer, or a ranking that
cannot separate events at any threshold.

We tested the first directly by re-selecting the threshold \emph{on the test
fold itself} --- an oracle no deployed system could use --- and recomputing
event recall at the same budget. It changed the result in \textbf{none} of
the six XGBoost fold~$\times$~condition cells. Threshold selection is
therefore not the binding constraint, and neither smoothing nor a finer
sweep can recover the missed events.

The binding constraint is the budget itself. Table~\ref{tab:frontier} sweeps
it, taking at each budget the best recall any threshold achieves on test.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Best achievable event recall for the XGBoost baseline as a function
of the false-alarm budget (mean over the three test folds). The
pre-registered operating point sits in the flat, uninformative region of the
curve.}
\label{tab:frontier}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
False alarms per hour & 0.01 & 0.10 & 0.25 & 0.50 \\
\midrule
\texttt{real\_only}      & 0.167 & 0.317 & 0.917 & 0.917 \\
\texttt{real\_plus\_sim} & 0.167 & 0.450 & 0.917 & 0.917 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Relaxing the budget from one alarm per 100~hours to one per four hours moves
recall from $0.167$ to $\mathbf{0.917}$. The events are separable; the
tolerance is what excludes them. The arithmetic is instance-level: at
$0.01$ alarms per hour a test fold with 523--855 Normal hours may emit only
5--9 false alarms across roughly 120 Normal recordings, so the 4--5 event
recordings must rank in the top few percent of \emph{all} recordings by peak
score.

This is a deployment trade-off rather than a defect. One alarm per four
hours is plausible for a supervised control room and implausible for an
unattended system, and the budget was fixed before the signal strength was
known. We therefore report the frontier alongside the single pre-registered
point; quoting only the latter would understate what the models detect, and
quoting only the former would hide the cost of getting there.

\subsubsection{Calibration}
Calibration behaved as intended in every fold and both conditions. Platt
scaling fit on validation reduced expected calibration error from $0.0409$
to $0.0106$ under \texttt{real\_only} and from $0.0538$ to $0.0121$ under
\texttt{real\_plus\_sim} (a 74--78\% reduction), and the Brier score by 29\%
in both, improving in all 6 fold~$\times$~condition cells. Because Module~8
selects the alarm threshold by sweeping a probability axis, this is a
prerequisite for that threshold to transfer, not a cosmetic step.
Fig.~\ref{fig:reliability} shows the before/after curves with a per-bin count
panel beneath; at a 3\% positive rate the high-probability bins hold very few
windows, and a reliability curve that hides bin populations makes a handful
of unlucky windows look like systematic miscalibration.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{reliability_xgboost.png}
\caption{Reliability of the XGBoost baseline on a validation fold, before
and after Platt scaling. Marker area and the lower panel both encode the
number of windows per bin.}
\label{fig:reliability}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Tuning budget}
The search evaluated the full 16-configuration grid per fold under grouped
inner CV, and both conditions of a fold share the configuration selected on
that fold's real training wells, so the two conditions differ only in
training data. Selected configurations were consistent
(\texttt{max\_depth}~$=3$, \texttt{n\_estimators}~$=300$ in both tunable
folds): the search preferred the smallest and shallowest models offered,
the expected outcome with roughly 1{,}400 positive windows.

% ---- VI-B. Deep Model Results (M4) ----
\subsection{Deep Models: TCN and GRU}
\label{sec:results_dl}

% TODO (M4): Write TCN and GRU results.
% - Same metrics as XGBoost, same two conditions
% - GRU bidirectional=False — note in text
% - Compare parameter counts, training time, VRAM peak

Table~\ref{tab:event_recall} shows that neither deep model achieved reliable event detection across all three folds. Under \texttt{real\_only}, the TCN detected one event in one fold (fold~1, lead time 89.3\,min), yielding a mean recall of $8.3\% \pm 14.4\%$. The GRU detected zero events under \texttt{real\_only} (mean recall $0.0\%$) and one event under \texttt{real\_plus\_sim} (mean recall $6.7\% \pm 11.5\%$).

Calibration was poor for both deep models. The TCN's expected calibration error (ECE) was $0.427 \pm 0.036$ under \texttt{real\_only} --- roughly an order of magnitude worse than XGBoost's Platt-scaled ECE of $0.095$. The GRU was better calibrated (ECE $0.094 \pm 0.022$) but this did not translate to detection: a calibrated model that produces low positive probabilities throughout still misses every event.

Early stopping was effective in limiting overfitting: the GRU converged in 11--25 epochs (best checkpoint at epoch 7--14) and the TCN in 11--29 epochs. Training time on the A100 GPU was under 5 minutes per model per fold. The deep model results confirm the finding from Section~\ref{sec:results_baserate}: with fold~0 containing a single positive validation window, threshold selection is conducted on noise, and the resulting threshold transfers poorly to the test fold regardless of model architecture.

\section{Discussion and Limitations}
\label{sec:discussion}

% TODO (M2): Write Discussion & Limitations. Must cover:
% - Only 14 positive events from 7 wells — statistical significance concern
% - 3 blockage instances — headline uses transient onset (Variant A)
% - Normal wells and hydrate wells are disjoint — generalization concern
% - Fold count given n=7 positive wells
% - Simulated data systematically over-represents blockage phase
% - SSL pretraining: "not attempted within the project timeframe"

\subsection{Sample Size Is the Dominant Limitation}
Every finding in this study is conditioned on a dataset with 14 real transient instances across 7 wells. With 3 outer folds, the largest test set contains 5 events and the smallest 4 --- not enough to compute a meaningful confidence interval on event recall, as the $\pm$ values in Table~\ref{tab:event_recall} already signal (the standard deviation equals or exceeds the mean for every model). The results presented here should be read as \emph{ordering evidence} (XGBoost $>$ TCN $>$ GRU, at this scale of data) rather than absolute performance claims.

\subsection{Disjoint Well Populations Limit Generalization}
The hydrate wells and normal-operation wells are completely disjoint, which means every test fold asks: ``can this model generalize to a well it has never seen in training?'' The feature-importance analysis in Section~\ref{sec:results_shortcut} shows that the XGBoost baseline partially answers this question by exploiting sensor missingness patterns (which well has which sensors) rather than physical pressure or temperature dynamics. This is a shortcut that will not generalize to a new well with a different instrumentation profile, and it also means the reported recall likely overstates the model's physical understanding of hydrate onset.

\subsection{Simulated Data Hurts More Than It Helps}
The \texttt{real\_plus\_sim} condition degraded XGBoost performance (mean recall $16.7\%$ vs.\ $23.3\%$ under \texttt{real\_only}) and did not help either deep model in a consistent way. The explanation is distributional: the simulated windows are 90.3\% positive against a 3.34\% real positive rate, effectively training the model on a world where hydrate events are nearly certain, then testing it on a world where they are rare. Calibration is disrupted, threshold selection targets a different operating point, and the model becomes over-sensitive on real normal-operation sequences.

\subsection{SSL Pretraining Not Attempted}
Self-supervised pretraining on the large unlabeled normal-operation segments (approximately 594 instances $\times$ 1{,}071 windows each) was identified as a promising direction to improve representations before supervised fine-tuning. It was not attempted within the project timeframe: the full supervised pipeline was completed and validated only shortly before the submission deadline, leaving no time for the additional infrastructure. This remains the highest-priority future direction.

\subsection{Fold~0 Threshold Selection Is Unreliable}
As noted in Section~\ref{sec:experimental_setup}, fold~0 has exactly one positive validation event. A threshold sweep over 200 candidate values selects the one that happens to detect that single event, with no ability to distinguish a genuinely good threshold from a lucky one. This structural flaw in fold~0 propagates to the test metrics: the XGBoost standard deviation of $\pm 25.2\%$ on event recall is driven almost entirely by the difference between fold~0 (0\%, no detections) and folds 1--2. With more positive wells this could be addressed by increasing the fold count; with 7 wells it cannot.


% ====================================================================
% VIII. CONCLUSION — M5 writes
% ====================================================================
\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We compared XGBoost, TCN, and GRU for early detection of hydrate formation in offshore well service lines using the 3W Dataset~2.0.0. All models were evaluated at a matched false-alarm budget of one alarm per 100 operating hours using grouped cross-validation with well-level splits.

XGBoost trained on real data only was the only model to achieve consistent detection, with a mean event recall of $23.3\% \pm 25.2\%$ and a mean lead time of $43.4$\,min across two detected folds. Deep models (TCN, GRU) did not achieve reliable detection, primarily because the training set contains only 14 real transient instances --- too few for gradient-based models to learn the transition dynamics without overfitting to well identity. Simulated data did not improve any model's test recall and degraded XGBoost's performance due to a severe distributional mismatch ($90.3\%$ positive rate in simulation vs.\ $3.34\%$ in real data).

Feature importance analysis revealed that the XGBoost baseline partly exploits sensor missingness patterns (which channels are instrumented on which well) rather than physical hydrate dynamics. This is a known shortcut in datasets with disjoint populations and instrumentation differences between event and non-event wells, and it limits the generalizability of the reported detection rate to wells with different sensor configurations.

The primary limitation of this study is sample size: 14 real transient events across 7 wells do not support statistically powerful conclusions about model ordering, and the $\pm$ values throughout the results section reflect this. Future work should prioritize acquiring more labeled real data, then investigate self-supervised pre-training on the large unlabeled normal-operation archive as a way to build better representations before supervised fine-tuning on the scarce positive examples.

Code, data processing scripts, and the complete evaluation pipeline are available at \url{https://github.com/AMammedova/team-hydrate3w} (tagged \texttt{v1.0-final}).
